record.paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
record.original_question: For trisections of 4-manifolds, determine analogues of Casson-Gordon theory for Heegaard splittings: identify properties of trisections that have strong topological consequences, such as simplifying the trisection or producing useful topological information, and that can be recognized from local information such as a trisection diagram.

evidence.quote: A key concept introduced in the theory by Casson and Gordon was the notion of strong irreducibility

The challenge for the analogous theory of trisections of 4-manifold is to determine properties of trisections that have strong topological consequences and that can be determined by local information, for instance, from a trisection diagram.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. A genus-$g$ Heegaard splitting of a closed orientable 3-manifold $Y$ is a decomposition $Y = H_1 \cup_\Sigma H_2$ into two genus-$g$ handlebodies glued along their common boundary surface $\Sigma$. Casson and Gordon called such a splitting strongly irreducible if every pair of essential disks $D_i \subset H_i$ has boundaries that intersect on $\Sigma$; this local, diagrammatic property has strong global topological consequences (e.g., incompressibility of $\Sigma$ when the splitting is irreducible but not strongly irreducible, and rigidity-type results).

A $(g;k_1,k_2,k_3)$-trisection of a closed orientable 4-manifold $X$ is a decomposition $X = X_1 \cup X_2 \cup X_3$ into three four-dimensional 1-handlebodies $X_i \cong 
atural^{k_i} S^1 	imes B^3$ such that each pairwise intersection $X_i \cap X_j$ is a 3-dimensional handlebody and the triple intersection $\Sigma = X_1 \cap X_2 \cap X_3$ is a closed orientable genus-$g$ surface. A trisection diagram is a tuple $(\Sigma; \alpha,  eta, \gamma)$ of three cut systems on $\Sigma$ encoding the trisection up to diffeomorphism.

Problem. Develop an analogue of Casson–Gordon theory for trisections of smooth, closed, orientable 4-manifolds. Concretely, identify and characterize properties of a trisection (analogous to strong irreducibility of a Heegaard splitting) which
  (i) can be detected from local data of a trisection diagram $(\Sigma;\alpha, eta,\gamma)$, and
  (ii) imply strong topological or combinatorial consequences for the trisection or for the underlying 4-manifold $X$ (for instance, forcing the trisection to simplify, bounding its genus, or yielding diffeomorphism-type information).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of developing a full Casson–Gordon-type theory for trisections remains an active research direction. Partial progress exists: analogues of the rectangle condition and notions of reducibility for trisection diagrams have been formulated, and recent work (e.g., arXiv:2509.11701, 2024–2025) studies whether such diagrammatic conditions detect strong irreducibility. However, no comprehensive analogue is established, so the problem appears still open.

status_evidence.title: The rectangle condition does not detect the strong irreducibility
status_evidence.snippet: Studies whether the rectangle condition (a Casson-Gordon style diagrammatic criterion) detects strong irreducibility, indicating ongoing research.
status_evidence.claim: Analogues of Casson-Gordon diagrammatic conditions are still being investigated; a full theory for trisections is not established.

status_evidence.title: Diagrammatic criteria for strong irreducibility of Heegaard splittings and finiteness of Goeritz groups
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work on diagrammatic criteria for strong irreducibility in the Heegaard setting, with relevance to trisection analogues.
status_evidence.claim: Active research on diagrammatic strong irreducibility criteria continues, with the trisection analogue not yet fully developed.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
status_evidence.snippet: Lists the development of Casson-Gordon analogues for trisections as an open challenge.
status_evidence.claim: Problem is listed as open in a problem-list document.
